articles.label: County Budget
articles.headline: Escambia County faces $12 million shortfall as tourism tax revenue drops
articles.dek: With beach renourishment and jail expansion on the line, commissioners must decide what gets cut before the July budget deadline.
brief: Tourist Development Tax collections fell 18% year-over-year through April, leaving Escambia County $12 million short of projected revenue.
Commissioners must finalize the FY2027 budget by July 15, forcing decisions on Pensacola Beach renourishment and the delayed jail expansion project.
County Administrator Wes Moreno has proposed delaying capital projects rather than cutting services, but commissioners remain divided on priorities.
articles.body:
The fourth-floor conference room in the Ernie Lee Magaha Government Building was standing room only Thursday morning. County employees lined the walls. A facilities manager checked his phone. Near the door, two sheriff's deputies in tan uniforms waited for their agenda item.

Escambia County Administrator Wes Moreno didn't soften the news.

"We are looking at a $12.2 million gap between projected revenues and planned expenditures," Moreno told the Board of County Commissioners. "That is not a rounding error. That requires decisions."

The shortfall stems primarily from a sharp decline in Tourist Development Tax collections, the bed tax paid by visitors staying at hotels, vacation rentals and campgrounds throughout the county. Through April, TDT revenue totaled $14.1 million—down 18% from the same period last year and well below the $19.8 million the county had budgeted.

Hurricane season fears kept visitors away last fall. A cooler-than-average spring didn't help. Neither did gas prices that peaked above $4 a gallon in March.

"People are still traveling," said Visit Pensacola President Darien Schaefer, who presented tourism data to commissioners earlier this month. "They're just not staying as long and they're not spending as much."

Two projects, not enough money

The timing couldn't be worse. Two major capital projects hang in the balance.

The Pensacola Beach renourishment project, delayed twice since 2023, was scheduled to begin construction this fall. The $28 million project would restore roughly 8 miles of shoreline from Fort Pickens to Portofino. The county's share—approximately $9 million—was earmarked from TDT reserves that no longer exist at projected levels.

Meanwhile, the Escambia County Jail expansion has been in planning for six years. The current facility, built in 1992, was designed for 1,200 inmates. It regularly holds more than 1,600. Federal monitors have cited overcrowding in three consecutive reports.

Sheriff Chip Simmons made his case Thursday in characteristically direct terms.

"I can't manufacture space," Simmons told commissioners. "Every week I'm making decisions about who stays and who gets released early. That's not public safety. That's crisis management."

The jail expansion carries a $47 million price tag. The county had planned to issue bonds this summer, with debt service payments beginning in FY2027. Those payments—roughly $3.8 million annually—were built into budget projections that assumed stronger revenue.

The administrator's proposal

Moreno's recommended approach: delay, don't cut.

His budget framework, distributed to commissioners Wednesday, proposes pushing the beach renourishment start date to spring 2027 and postponing the jail bond issuance by one year. No layoffs. No service reductions. No cuts to the sheriff's operational budget.

"We weather this year, tourism rebounds, and we're back on track," Moreno said. "That's the theory."

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh wasn't buying it.

"We've been saying 'next year' on the jail for half a decade," Bergosh said. "At what point do we admit we've got a structural problem, not a timing problem?"

Bergosh pointed to the county's growing reliance on TDT revenue to fund projects that benefit residents, not just tourists. State law restricts bed tax spending to tourism promotion and tourism-related infrastructure. The beach qualifies. The jail does not.

"We've backed ourselves into a corner," he said. "We need the beaches pretty so the tourists come so we can afford to fix the beaches. Meanwhile, our actual residents are dealing with an overcrowded jail and we can't touch that money."

Dividing lines

The five-member commission appears split.

Commissioner Lumon May, whose District 3 includes much of the county's lower-income population, said he won't support any budget that delays the jail.

"When we talk about who's in that facility, we're talking about my constituents' sons and brothers," May said. "They deserve humane conditions regardless of what they did."

Commissioner Mike Kohler, representing the beach and Perdido Key areas, argued the renourishment can't wait.

"Every storm season we delay is another season those properties flood," Kohler said. "Those property owners pay taxes too. They're watching their investments erode into the Gulf."

Commission Chair Robert Bender has scheduled a budget workshop for June 12. The board must adopt a tentative budget by July 15 to meet state deadlines.

Bender declined to state his position Thursday but acknowledged the difficulty ahead.

"There's no version of this where everyone's happy," Bender said after the meeting. "We're going to make someone mad. The question is whether we make the right people mad."

What the numbers show

The revenue decline follows three years of record tourism. Escambia County collected $21.4 million in TDT revenue in FY2024, the highest in its history. Officials built subsequent budgets assuming that growth would continue, if not accelerate.

It didn't.

County budget documents show TDT collections have now fallen below pre-pandemic levels for three consecutive months. April's total—$3.1 million—was the lowest for that month since 2019.

The broader county budget isn't in crisis. Property tax revenue remains stable. Sales tax collections are flat but holding. The general fund shows adequate reserves.

But TDT money is siloed. It can't backfill other priorities. And the projects that depend on it are now competing for a smaller pool.

"Tourism is a volatile revenue source," said Amy Bates, the county's budget director. "We've known that. We planned for fluctuations. We didn't plan for a cliff."

What happens next

The June 12 workshop will be the first public forum where commissioners discuss specific tradeoffs. Moreno said his staff is preparing three budget scenarios: one that prioritizes beach renourishment, one that prioritizes the jail and one that delays both.

Public comment will be accepted at the workshop. Residents can also submit written comments through the county's website through June 10.

The final budget hearing is scheduled for September 15.

In the meantime, the beaches continue to erode and the jail continues to fill.

"We're not going to solve thirty years of underinvestment in one budget cycle," Moreno said. "But we have to start somewhere. That's what July is for."

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Bluffs project breaks ground after three years of delays
articles.dek: Construction crews finally moved dirt this week on the long-stalled mixed-use development at Main and Garden. Neighbors are watching to see if the affordable housing promises hold.
brief: Construction began Wednesday on The Bluffs, a 240-unit mixed-use project at Main Street and Garden Street that has been stalled since 2023
Developer Emerald Coast Partners says 20% of units will rent at affordable rates, but the commitment is not legally binding
The project received $2.3 million in city incentives tied to job creation and infrastructure improvements
articles.body:
The excavator bit into red clay Wednesday morning at the corner of Main and Garden, and a small crowd gathered on the sidewalk to watch. Some held phones. Others held coffee. A woman in scrubs on her way to Baptist leaned against a crepe myrtle and said what several neighbors have been thinking for three years: "I'll believe it when I see walls."

The Bluffs, a seven-story mixed-use development that Pensacola City Council approved in November 2022, has finally broken ground. The $67 million project from Emerald Coast Partners will bring 240 residential units, 12,000 square feet of ground-floor retail and a 340-space parking garage to a block that has sat vacant since the demolition of the old Escambia County health department building in 2019.

It has also brought three years of delays, two lawsuits, a change in general contractors and persistent questions about whether the affordable housing component will survive contact with reality.

What was promised

When developer Marcus Whitfield first presented the project to council, he called it "a new model for downtown living." The pitch included 48 units—20% of the total—reserved for renters earning 80% or less of the area median income. For a single person in Escambia County, that currently means an income of roughly $47,000 per year.

Those units would rent for approximately $1,100 per month for a one-bedroom, compared to market-rate units in the building projected at $1,650 and up.

The promise helped secure $2.3 million in city incentives: $1.5 million from the Community Redevelopment Agency for infrastructure improvements and $800,000 in property tax rebates tied to job creation benchmarks.

But the affordable housing commitment exists only in a nonbinding letter of intent attached to the CRA agreement. It is not recorded in the deed. It carries no penalty for noncompliance.

"We fully intend to honor that commitment," Whitfield said Wednesday, standing near the excavation site in a hard hat. "The economics still work. We're not backing away from it."

What changed

The project was supposed to open in late 2024. Instead, it spent most of that year in Escambia County Circuit Court.

First came a dispute with the original general contractor, Gulf States Construction, over cost overruns tied to post-pandemic material prices. That lawsuit settled in March 2024 for undisclosed terms. Then came a challenge from the Pensacola Historic Preservation Society, which argued the building's height and massing violated design standards in the Palafox Historic Business District. A judge dismissed that suit in September 2024, ruling the project site sits outside the district's boundaries.

Through it all, construction financing dried up. Whitfield told The Flightline that his original lender, a regional bank based in Mobile, pulled out in early 2025 citing "market uncertainty." A new financing package closed in February with a Miami-based private equity fund.

The terms of that deal are not public. But filings with the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation show the project's total capitalization increased from $67 million to $74 million between the original 2022 application and the current permit.

Who's watching

The Tanyard neighborhood sits just north of the construction site, across a set of railroad tracks that still carry CSX freight trains through downtown. It is one of the oldest Black neighborhoods in Pensacola, and one of the few remaining affordable pockets in the urban core.

At a Tanyard Neighborhood Association meeting Tuesday night, residents spent 40 minutes discussing The Bluffs before moving to other agenda items.

"Every time they build something new down here, rents go up over here," said Clarence Washington, 71, who has lived on North DeVilliers Street since 1978. "I'm not against development. I'm against being pushed out."

Association president Denise Holloway said she had requested a meeting with Whitfield to discuss local hiring commitments and the affordable unit timeline. As of Tuesday, she had not received a response.

Whitfield said Wednesday he would "absolutely" meet with the association. "We want to be good neighbors," he said. "That's part of being in this community."

What happens next

The construction timeline calls for vertical work to begin in August, with the parking structure completed by spring 2027 and the residential tower topped out by fall of that year. First occupancy is projected for early 2028.

Pensacola City Council member Teniade Broughton, whose District 6 includes the project site, said she plans to introduce a resolution in June requiring annual compliance reports on any city-incentivized development with affordable housing commitments.

"We gave them public money based on public promises," Broughton said. "The public deserves to know if those promises are being kept."

The resolution would not apply retroactively to The Bluffs. But Broughton said she hoped it would set a precedent.

Meanwhile, the excavator kept running Wednesday morning. By noon, the pit was four feet deep. The woman in scrubs had long since left for her shift. The coffee drinkers had moved on. But a few neighbors remained, watching the dirt pile up on the sidewalk.

Walls are still a long way off.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 200,000 visitors and a logistics nightmare
articles.dek: Hotels are booked through Gulf Breeze. Traffic on the Three Mile Bridge will be brutal. Here's what residents need to know before the crowds arrive.
brief: The Blue Angels homecoming air show at NAS Pensacola runs July 10-11, with practice sessions July 8-9 open to the public
Hotel occupancy across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties is projected at 98% for the weekend, with nightly rates averaging $289
Escambia County Sheriff's Office will implement contraflow on the Three Mile Bridge during peak departure hours Sunday afternoon
articles.body:
The parking lot at Joe Patti's Seafood was nearly empty at 7 a.m. on a Tuesday in late May. By this time next month, every square foot of asphalt from here to Perdido Key will be claimed territory.

The Blue Angels are coming home.

NAS Pensacola's annual homecoming air show, scheduled for July 10-11, will draw an estimated 200,000 spectators to the base over two days. Another 50,000 are expected to watch from Pensacola Beach, Fort Pickens, and boats anchored in the bay. The economic impact is projected at $45 million. The traffic impact is projected at miserable.

"This is our Super Bowl," said Visit Pensacola President Dana Young. "And just like the Super Bowl, it requires the entire community to execute."

The hotel situation

It's already too late for a room downtown.

As of Friday, hotel occupancy for the weekend of July 10-11 stood at 94% across Escambia County, according to Visit Pensacola data. Santa Rosa County wasn't far behind at 91%. By the time the F/A-18 Super Hornets make their first practice pass on Wednesday, July 8, those numbers will approach total capacity.

Average nightly rates have climbed to $289, up from $187 during the same weekend last year. The Margaritaville Beach Hotel on Pensacola Beach is sold out at $459 per night. The Hampton Inn on Airport Boulevard, 12 miles from the base, is asking $219.

Short-term rentals on Pensacola Beach are commanding $600 to $1,200 per night for properties that rent for half that in June.

"We started getting calls in February," said Marcus Chen, general manager of the Hilton Pensacola Beach. "By April, we were turning people away."

The overflow is pushing into Gulf Breeze, Navarre, and as far east as Fort Walton Beach. Some visitors have booked rooms in Mobile, 60 miles west, and plan to commute.

Getting there and getting out

The math is simple and brutal. NAS Pensacola has two public entry points. The base can accommodate roughly 15,000 vehicles. The show draws 100,000 people per day.

Gates open at 8 a.m. both days. The Blue Angels take the sky at 2 p.m. The smart money arrives by 9.

"If you're crossing the Three Mile Bridge at noon, you're going to watch the show from your car," said Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons at a press briefing Thursday. "I'm not being dramatic. That's just the reality."

Simmons announced that ECSO will implement contraflow traffic patterns on the Pensacola Bay Bridge—three lanes outbound, one lane inbound—from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Sunday, July 11. The measure, used successfully during Hurricane Sally evacuations, will be the first deployment for a planned event.

Additional traffic control measures include:

  • No left turns from Navy Boulevard onto Blue Angel Parkway from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. both days
  • Temporary traffic signals at the intersection of Navy Boulevard and Corry Station Road
  • Pensacola Beach access restricted to residents and hotel guests with proof of reservation from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday
  • Free satellite parking at Pensacola Bay Center with continuous shuttle service to the base

The shuttle system, operated by ECAT, will run 40 buses on a continuous loop from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Round-trip fare is $5. Officials are strongly encouraging its use.

"We can move 20,000 people on those buses," said ECAT Director Albee Pickett. "Or those same 20,000 people can sit in a four-mile backup on Navy Boulevard. Their choice."

What the base is doing

NAS Pensacola Commanding Officer Capt. Terrence Shashaty outlined base preparations during a media tour Wednesday. Temporary bleachers will add 8,000 seats to the flight line viewing area. Food vendors will number 47, up from 32 last year. Hydration stations will be placed every 200 yards.

The base is also expanding its medical footprint. Three field hospitals will operate near the viewing areas, staffed by Navy corpsmen and civilian EMTs. Last year's show saw 127 heat-related medical calls. Base officials are planning for 200.

"July in Pensacola is not forgiving," Shashaty said. "We will have shade structures, we will have water, we will have medical. But people need to take this seriously. Hydrate before you come. Wear sunscreen. Know your limits."

The base will be dry—no alcohol sales or consumption on the installation. Coolers are permitted but will be searched at entry. Prohibited items include drones, pets, weapons, and chairs taller than 36 inches.

The economic engine

For all the logistical headaches, homecoming week is the single largest economic event in Escambia County's calendar. The $45 million projected impact doesn't include the ancillary spending that radiates outward.

McGuire's Irish Pub on Gregory Street is hiring 25 temporary staff. The Fish House on Bayfront Parkway has reserved its entire waterfront patio for a ticketed viewing event at $150 per person. Uber and Lyft have sent notifications to drivers across three states, promising surge pricing and bonuses.

"I make more money in these two days than any other two-week stretch of the year," said David Maldonado, who operates a food truck on Pensacola Beach. "You deal with the crowds because you have to. They pay the bills."

The Blue Angels themselves are Pensacola's most effective marketing asset. The team's presence at NAS Pensacola, their home since 1954, draws year-round tourism to the National Naval Aviation Museum—which sees 750,000 annual visitors—and generates a continuous trickle of aviation enthusiasts who come simply to watch practice sessions.

Homecoming week concentrates that attention into 96 hours.

For residents: hunker down or cash in

Locals tend to fall into two camps during homecoming week. Some flee. Others monetize.

The Pensacola Beach RV Resort is fully booked with residents from Pensacola proper who rent out their homes for the weekend and camp on the island. One couple from East Hill told The Flightline they net $2,400 after listing their three-bedroom bungalow on Airbnb.

"We bring the dog, we bring a cooler, we watch the show from the campground," said the husband, who asked not to be named to avoid attention from his homeowners' association. "Best weekend of the year."

Others simply leave. Destin, Panama City Beach, and Gulf Shores see noticeable upticks in Escambia County license plates during homecoming weekend. Some residents make it an annual tradition—the inverse of the tourist influx.

For those who stay, preparation is key. Grocery stores in the downtown corridor will be crowded. Gas stations on Navy Boulevard will have lines. Restaurants without reservations will have waits measured in hours, not minutes.

"Do your shopping by Wednesday," advised longtime Pensacola Beach resident Carla Morrison, who has lived through 23 homecoming shows. "Fill your tank by Wednesday. Then stay home and watch from your balcony like a sane person."

The Blue Angels practice sessions on July 8-9 are open to the public at no charge and draw significantly smaller crowds—typically 15,000 to 20,000 per day. For residents seeking the experience without the crush, that's the window.

The show itself

None of it would matter if the show weren't worth seeing. It is.

The Blue Angels' 2026 demonstration will feature the full six-jet delta formation, the signature opposing solo maneuvers, and the sneak pass that still makes crowds flinch after 80 years. The team will be flying the F/A-18 Super Hornet for the fifth consecutive season, having transitioned from the legacy Hornet in 2021.

Civilian performers include the U.S. Army Golden Knights parachute team, aerobatic pilot Rob Holland, and a WWII-era warbird demonstration featuring a restored P-51 Mustang from the Commemorative Air Force.

Gates open at 8 a.m. The civilian acts begin at 10. The Blue Angels take the sky at 2 p.m. and fly for approximately 45 minutes.

And then, as quickly as it began, the jets return to the hangar, the crowds disperse to their cars, and the Three Mile Bridge becomes a parking lot.

"It's chaos," Sheriff Simmons acknowledged. "Beautiful, American, loud-as-hell chaos. That's what homecoming is."

Pensacola will spend the next six weeks preparing. The jets will be ready. The question is whether the infrastructure will be.
